title: When Artificial Intelligence Leaves the Screen
excerpt: For years, robots have been programmed to perform repetitive tasks in controlled environments. Artificial intelligence is beginning to change that. Robots are learning to interpret their surroundings, understand instructions and adapt to situations they haven't encountered before. Could we be approaching a future where robots become a much more familiar part of everyday life?
content:
For years, most of our conversations about artificial intelligence have centred on what happens on a screen. We've watched AI learn to write, generate images, analyse information, understand speech and answer increasingly complicated questions.

Now AI is starting to leave the screen. It's giving robots the ability to interpret what's happening around them, understand what they're being asked to do and decide how to do it, rather than simply follow a fixed set of instructions. If that keeps developing, it could change a lot about how we work, live and use technology.

## Robots have been around for decades

Robots aren't new. Factories have used them for decades to weld, paint, assemble components and move materials around.

They're very good at those jobs. A robot arm can repeat the same movement thousands of times with remarkable speed and precision, but only inside a carefully controlled environment. Traditional industrial robots follow predefined instructions and expect everything to be where it's supposed to be. Move an object slightly out of position, put an obstacle in the way or change the task, and the robot may struggle. It can follow instructions without understanding what they're for.

## Giving robots a brain

Imagine asking a robot to tidy a room.

A traditional robot would need a detailed, programmed sequence of actions: where each object is, how to pick it up, where to put it and what to do if something goes wrong.

An AI-powered robot could use cameras and sensors to take in the room, recognise the objects in it, interpret your instructions and work out what to do and in what order. If something didn't go to plan, it could reassess and try another approach.

This is what people usually mean by physical AI or embodied AI: intelligence that uses what it understands to act in the physical world. It brings together several areas of AI and robotics:

- Vision, to recognise objects, people and surroundings.
- Language, to understand spoken or written instructions.
- Reasoning, to work out what needs to happen and in what order.
- Movement, to control the motors, joints, hands and other mechanisms that carry out the task.
- Learning, to improve and adapt to new situations.

Put together, these could make robots far more flexible than the machines we're used to.

## What can robots actually do today?

It's easy to get carried away by videos of humanoid robots walking, dancing and picking things up. I find the less flashy work more interesting: robots being asked to do something useful.

Google DeepMind has been developing its Gemini Robotics models, which connect language and visual understanding to physical actions. Its 2026 work includes robots carrying out more complex sequences of movements, handling objects with greater dexterity and coordinating with other robots. The aim is for a robot to understand a task and work out for itself how to complete it.

Manufacturing is where practical applications are starting to show up. BMW has worked with Figure AI to test humanoid robots in production. During a pilot at BMW's Spartanburg plant, a Figure 02 robot handled sheet-metal parts for vehicle production, moving more than 90,000 components over roughly 1,250 operating hours. Other companies are trying robots for moving materials, handling containers and supporting production logistics.

Factories make sense as a starting point because they're relatively structured. A production line is far more predictable than someone's home, where every room and object is different. Even so, many of these projects are still pilots or controlled deployments. General-purpose robots can't yet reliably take on any task you give them.

## Why do robots need to look human?

People often ask why so many companies are building humanoid robots. Wouldn't it be easier to build a machine designed for the job?

In many cases, yes. A robotic arm is usually better at repetitive assembly work, and a wheeled robot moves goods around a warehouse more efficiently. A specialised machine will often be cheaper, faster and more reliable than a humanoid.

But most of the world is designed for people. Homes, workplaces, tools, doors, stairs and vehicles are all built around the human body, so a robot with two arms and two legs could work in places nobody adapted for robots. If the long-term goal is a machine that can work across lots of human environments, that's a real advantage, even if a humanoid isn't the right answer for every job.

Boston Dynamics, Figure AI and Tesla are all taking different approaches to humanoid robotics. Whatever the approach, they all have to build a machine that moves safely, handles objects reliably and understands what it's doing.

## Could robots become part of everyday life?

Factories and warehouses are the logical place to start, but the longer-term possibilities go much further. At home, a robot could help with household tasks, carry shopping, prepare simple meals or support someone with limited mobility. In healthcare, robots could take on physically demanding work, support rehabilitation or help people with everyday activities. In dangerous places, they could carry out inspections, handle hazardous materials or go where it isn't safe for people. Agriculture, construction, logistics and maintenance all have uses too.

Some of this already exists in specialised forms. The bigger ambition is a robot that can adapt to many tasks instead of needing a different machine for each one. That flexibility is what AI could add.

## There are still some big challenges

There's still a considerable gap between an impressive demonstration and a robot that can work reliably alongside people every day.

Reliability is a major issue. A robot that completes a task nine times out of ten may not be good enough for a factory, a hospital or a home.

Dexterity is another. Human hands are remarkably sophisticated. Picking up a box is fairly straightforward, but handling delicate objects, tying shoelaces or preparing food needs much finer control.

Safety matters more here than it does on a screen. When a chatbot gets something wrong, you get a bad answer. When a physical machine makes the wrong decision while moving around people, someone could get hurt.

There are also open questions about cost, maintenance, battery life, privacy, and what a robot should do when it meets something it doesn't understand.

The biggest challenge may be adaptability. The real world is messy and unpredictable, and coping with it is much harder than performing a carefully rehearsed demonstration.

## A different kind of technological revolution?

This area interests me because it changes how we think about AI. Most of the progress so far has been about making computers better at processing and understanding information. Now that intelligence is being connected to machines that can act in the physical world. It also connects with the progress in multimodal AI: teaching computers to see, hear and understand was the first part, and giving them the ability to act on that understanding is the next.

I don't expect we'll all have a humanoid robot doing the housework next year. There's a huge amount of engineering still to do before that's realistic. But I do think robots are becoming more adaptable and more useful, and less confined to carefully controlled environments.

We've spent decades teaching computers to understand the world, and now we're starting to let them do something in it. That could turn out to be one of the most significant developments in AI so far.
